FULL SOLUTION

Worked steps

  1. List the forces: gravity mg down, normal force N perpendicular to the ramp, and tension T up the ramp. There is no friction.
  2. Choose axes: take +x uphill, +y outward perpendicular to the incline.
  3. Break weight into components: parallel component mg sin 15° acts downhill. Perpendicular component mg cos 15° acts inward.
  4. Along the ramp: the object is stationary, so ΣFₓ = 0 and T − mg sin 15° = 0. Therefore T = (1,410)(9.81)sin 15° ≈ 3,580 N.
  5. Perpendicular to the ramp: ΣFᵧ = 0 and N − mg cos 15° = 0. Therefore N = (1,410)(9.81)cos 15° ≈ 13,361 N.
  6. Conclusion: a cable tension of approximately 3.58 × 10³ N, directed uphill, holds the object at rest. The answer matches the handwritten result when using g = 9.81 m/s².
Small correction to the handwritten FBD: do not include both the full mg and its perpendicular component in the same perpendicular-force equation. Resolve gravity into two components, then use N − mg cos θ = 0. The tension equation, T = mg sin θ, is correct.

Worked steps

Part (b) uses tan⁻¹ because it finds the direction of the resulting ground velocity. Part (c) uses sin⁻¹ because it finds the heading needed to cancel the current.

Forgetting is part of memory.

TED Talk summary — Richard Morris

Focus: hippocampusMemory and forgettingLearning reflection
“

Summary

In the TED Talk Forgetting Is a Part of Memory, Richard Morris explains that forgetting is a normal part of how the brain works. He describes how the hippocampus helps us form memories and why some experiences stay with us while others fade over time.

He also explains that memories are often stronger when an experience is surprising, emotional, or different from everyday life. Using examples and experiments, he shows that everyone forgets information and that the brain is not designed to hold on to every detail.

The main message is that forgetting is not always a negative thing. It can help the brain focus on what matters and make room for new learning.

Connection to studying

This idea connects to how I study math and physics: reviewing concepts, working through examples, and testing what I remember can show me which steps I understand and which ones still need practice.

MAIN IDEAS

Three takeaways

  • Forgetting is normal. Memory is selective rather than permanent.
  • The hippocampus matters. It plays an important role in creating memories.
  • Experiences stand out. Emotional and unusual events may be easier to remember.

Reflection based on the supplied TED Talk notes.

FULL LAB REPORTSPH4U · OCTOBER 2026

Unit 1 Dynamics

( video at the end )

Information

  • Course Code: SPH4U

  • Unit: Dynamics

  • Student Names: Jaspreet, Sekhon, Aditya Walia, Prabh Arora

  • Date: October 2026

Abstract

This experiment investigated the dynamics of uniform circular motion by examining the quantitative relationships between revolving mass (m), orbital radius (r), period of revolution (T), frequency (f), tangential velocity (v), centripetal acceleration (ac), and centripetal force (Fc). Data was collected across two distinct radi (r₁ = 30 cm, r₂ = 60 cm) and three varying masses (m₁ = 12.9 g, m₂ = 19.2 g, m₃ = 26.33 g) by timing 20 complete revolutions.

Empirical periods ranged from 0.375 s to 0.618 s, with corresponding frequencies between 1.62 Hz and 2.67 Hz. Increasing the radius consistently increased the period across all masses by a ratio of 1.18 to 1.36 (averaging 1.25), supporting the qualitative directional trend of T being proportional to √r (theoretical ratio 1.41), though falling short of theoretical ideal constant-force scaling. Mass variations demonstrated an expected period increase at 60 cm (0.486 s to 0.511 s to 0.618 s), but contained an anomaly at 30 cm (19.2 g yielded T = 0.375 s, faster than 12.9 g at T = 0.406 s). Back-calculation revealed that tension was not constant, ranging from 0.93 N to 1.74 N. The findings confirm that manual rotation fails to hold tension constant, necessitating fixed hanging counterweights for true single-variable control.

Introduction and Theoretical Background

Uniform circular motion describes the movement of an object along a circular path at constant speed v. Although the magnitude of the velocity vector remains constant, its direction changes continuously. Because velocity is a vector, a continuous change in direction constitutes an acceleration. This acceleration is directed radially inward toward the center of curvature and is defined as centripetal acceleration (ac):

ac = v² / r

For an object traveling a path circumference C = 2πr during a period T, tangential velocity is:

v = 2πr / T = 2πrf

Substituting v into the centripetal acceleration expression yields:

ac = 4π²r f² = 4π²r / T²

According to Newton's Second Law (F_net = m · a), any accelerating mass requires an unbalanced net force in the direction of acceleration. The required net inward force for circular motion is the centripetal force (Fc):

Fc = m · ac = m v² / r = 4π²m r f² = 4π²m r / T²

Rearranging this theoretical framework yields explicit functions for period (T) and frequency (f) under constant force conditions:

T = 2π √(m r / Fc)

f = (1 / 2π) √(Fc / (m r))

From these derivations, three theoretical power-law relationships emerge when other parameters are controlled:

  • T is proportional to √r (or f is proportional to r⁻¹/²)

  • T is proportional to √m (or f is proportional to m⁻¹/²)

  • f is proportional to √Fc (or T is proportional to Fc⁻¹/²)

Purpose

To determine how the mass of a whirled object and the radius of its circular path affect its period and frequency, and to evaluate the experimental results against the centripetal-force model Fc = 4π²m r f².

Hypotheses

Radius Hypothesis:

If orbital radius (r) is doubled while maintaining a constant mass and force, the period (T) will increase by a factor of √2 ≈ 1.41, and frequency (f) will decrease by 1/√2 ≈ 0.707.

Justification: From T = 2π √(m r / Fc), T scales directly with √r. Doubling path length increases revolution time when tangential speed does not scale proportionally.

Mass Hypothesis:

If revolving mass (m) is increased at a constant radius and force, the period (T) will increase proportionally to √m.

Justification: Greater inertia resists directional acceleration (ac = Fc / m). At equal tension, a larger mass accelerates more slowly inward, requiring more time per orbit.

Force Hypothesis:

If centripetal force (Fc) increases at fixed mass and radius, frequency (f) will increase proportionally to √Fc.

Justification: A stronger net inward force produces greater centripetal acceleration, driving higher rotational speed and frequency.

Variables

Independent Variables:

  • Mass of Stopper (m): 12.9 g, 19.2 g, 26.33 g (±0.01 g)

  • Orbital Radius (r): 30 cm, 60 cm (±0.5 cm)

Dependent Variables:

  • Time for 20 Revolutions (t₂₀): Stopwatch measurement (±0.2 s human reaction error)

Derived Variables:

  • Period (T), Frequency (f), Tangential Speed (v), Centripetal Acceleration (ac), Centripetal Force (Fc): Calculated via kinematics and uniform circular motion force equations

Controlled Variables:

  • Revolution Count (N): Fixed at exactly 20 complete revolutions per trial

  • Apparatus & Operator: Same tubing, string, and operator across all trials

Uncontrolled Variables:

  • Tension / Centripetal Force (Fc): Unmeasured and uncontrolled directly during trials; dependent on hand rotation speed and back-calculated post-trial.

Materials & Apparatus

  • Glass or plastic guiding tube with smooth polished edges

  • Non-stretch cord/string (~1 m)

  • Rubber stoppers (12.9 g, 19.2 g, 26.33 g)

  • Precision digital electronic balance (±0.01 g)

  • Metre stick (±0.001 m)

  • Digital stopwatch (±0.01 s precision, ±0.2 s human reaction error)

Safety Precautions

  1. Clear Perimeter: Establish a 2-metre clearance radius around the operator to avoid hitting surrounding individuals or equipment.

  2. Eye Protection: Wear safety goggles at all times to protect against string breakage or mass detachment.

  3. Secure Attachment: Ensure stoppers are secured with double knots prior to every trial.

  4. Controlled Rotation: Maintain steady rotation above head level to prevent downward sagging or erratic trajectories.

Procedure

  1. Measure and record the mass of each rubber stopper using the electronic balance.

  2. Thread the string through the guide tube and knot the stopper firmly to one end.

  3. Measure string length from the top of the guide tube to the center of mass of the stopper, setting r₁ = 30 cm. Secure a reference marker on the string directly below the tube exit.

  4. Whirl the stopper in a horizontal circular path above head level, adjusting rotational speed until the reference marker remains stationary at the bottom of the tube.

  5. Allow the rotation to reach a steady state. Start the stopwatch as the stopper passes a fixed reference point, count 20 full revolutions, and stop timing. Record t₂₀.

  6. Repeat step 5 for three total trials per condition.

  7. Repeat steps 3 to 6 for the all masses at r = 30 cm.

  8. Adjust string length to r₂ = 60 cm and repeat steps 3 to 7 for all three masses.

Analysis & Sample Calculations

Sample Calculations (for m = 12.9 g = 0.0129 kg, r = 30 cm = 0.30 m):

Mean Time (t_avg):
t_avg = (7.77 + 8.35 + 8.22) / 3 = 8.1133 s ≈ 8.11 s

Period (T):
T = t_avg / N = 8.1133 / 20 = 0.40567 s ≈ 0.406 s

Frequency (f):
f = 1 / T = 20 / 8.1133 = 2.4651 Hz ≈ 2.47 Hz

Tangential Speed (v):
v = 2πr / T = 2 · π · 0.30 · 2.4651 = 4.6466 m/s ≈ 4.65 m/s

Centripetal Acceleration (ac):
ac = v² / r = (4.6466)² / 0.30 = 71.97 m/s² ≈ 72.0 m/s²

Centripetal Force (Fc):
Fc = m · ac = 0.0129 · 71.97 = 0.9284 N ≈ 0.93 N

Radius Scaling Ratios (T_60cm / T_30cm):

  • 12.9 g Stopper: 0.486 / 0.406 = 1.20 → Exponent n = ln(1.20) / ln(2) ≈ 0.26

  • 19.2 g Stopper: 0.511 / 0.375 = 1.36 → Exponent n = ln(1.36) / ln(2) ≈ 0.44

  • 26.33 g Stopper: 0.618 / 0.525 = 1.18 → Exponent n = ln(1.18) / ln(2) ≈ 0.24

Discussion

The experimental data confirms the directional claims of Hypotheses 1 and 2: expanding radius or increasing mass increases period and decreases frequency. However, the observed period ratios fall short of ideal constant-force theoretical scaling (T proportional to r^0.5 and T proportional to m^0.5).

At 30 cm, the 19.2 g mass produced a mean trial time of 7.49 s (T = 0.375 s), moving faster than the lighter 12.9 g stopper (T = 0.406 s). Back-calculating centripetal force reveals why: Fc for the 19.2 g mass reached 1.62 N, compared to 0.93 N for 12.9 g. Because tension was applied manually without a fixed counterweight, the operator spun the 19.2 g mass with 74% more force, pulling it faster and masking the theoretical mass-dependent inertia trend.

Newton's Laws in Circular Motion

  • Newton's First Law (Inertia): An object in motion maintains a constant velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. In UCM, the stopper's instantaneous velocity is tangential. If the string snaps or is released, centripetal tension drops to zero instantly, and the stopper flies off along a straight line tangent to the circle, not radially outward.

  • Newton's Second Law (F_net = m · a): Because the stopper continuously changes velocity direction, it undergoes inward centripetal acceleration ac. Newton's Second Law dictates that an unbalanced net inward force (Fc = m · ac) must act continuously toward the center.

  • Newton's Third Law & The "Centrifugal Force" Fallacy: Newton's Third Law states that every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force.

    • Action: String pulls inward on the stopper (Centripetal Force, acting on the stopper).

    • Reaction: Stopper pulls outward on the string/hand (Reaction Force, acting on the string/hand).

The outward pull felt by the operator's hand is a real force acting on the hand, not on the stopper. "Centrifugal force" is a fictitious inertia effect that appears only when observing motion from a rotating frame of reference. In an inertial ground frame, no outward force acts on the stopper.

Error Analysis & Improvements

Table 3: Experimental Uncertainties and Proposed Improvements

Error Source Type Effect on Experimental Results Proposed Practical Improvement
Uncontrolled Tension (Fc) Systematic Manual rotation causes tension variations (0.93 to 1.74 N), altering period scaling exponents. Attach a hanging mass (m_hang · g) to maintain constant, quantifiable tension.
Stopwatch Reaction Time Random Human delay (±0.2 s) introduces ~2-5% error on 8-12 s timings. Use photogates or high-frame-rate video analysis (60 fps).
Non-Horizontal Plane (String Sag) Systematic Gravity pulls the mass downward, causing string sag. True orbital radius is r_true = r · sin(θ) < r. Use a mechanical motor apparatus with a fixed horizontal rigid arm guide.
Small Sample Size (N=3) Statistical Standard deviations (0.30 to 0.94 s) make overlapping confidence intervals indistinguishable. Record 5-10 trials per condition to narrow standard error.

Real-World Application

In Olympic speed skating, an athlete of mass m rounding a curve of radius r at speed v requires a net centripetal force Fc = m v² / r. Because centripetal force depends on speed squared (v²), doubling cornering speed quadruples the required inward force. This force is provided by lateral friction between blade edges and ice, combined with leaning inward so normal force provides a horizontal component (FN · sin(θ)). If v exceeds available friction, the skater loses traction and slides tangentially off the track.

Conclusion

This experiment confirmed the qualitative dynamics of uniform circular motion: expanding radius or mass increases period and reduces frequency. Increasing radius from 30 cm to 60 cm increased the period by an average factor of 1.25. However, numerical scaling exponents (~0.31) diverged from ideal constant-force predictions (0.50). Back-calculating centripetal forces (0.93 N to 1.74 N) identified manual tension variation as the primary systematic limitation. Replacing manual rotation with hanging counterweights and photogate timing will isolate true single-variable control in future trials.

Abstract

This experiment investigated the dynamics of projectile motion by evaluating the impact of launch angle (θ = 25°, 40°, 55°) and vertical launch-to-landing displacement (Δy = 0 m, -0.75 m, +0.40 m) on horizontal range (R). A spring-loaded mini projectile launcher was used to fire a steel ball across three distinct experimental setups: Desk-to-Desk (Δy = 0 m), Desk-to-Ground (Δy = -0.75 m), and Ground-to-Desk (Δy = +0.40 m). Using the equal-height range equation on Desk-to-Desk trials, the baseline initial launch velocity was calculated as v₀ = 6.81 m/s ± 0.10 m/s.

For Desk-to-Desk launches, maximum horizontal range occurred at 40° (4.57 m ± 0.055 m), closely matching theoretical predictions (4.66 m, -1.9% error). For Desk-to-Ground launches, additional fall height extended flight time, increasing ranges across all angles and yielding a maximum range at 40° (5.34 m ± 0.055 m, -1.5% error). For Ground-to-Desk launches, upward vertical displacement reduced total flight time, decreasing horizontal ranges across all angles, with a maximum range at 40° (3.80 m ± 0.055 m, -7.7% error). Overall, experimental results agreed with two-dimensional kinematic theory within 1.5% to 11.2%. Discrepancies were primarily attributed to systematic factors, including aerodynamic drag and muzzle release height offset, rather than random measurement spread.

Introduction

Projectile motion describes the path of an object launched into two-dimensional space that moves under the influence of gravity, assuming air resistance is negligible. Under ideal conditions, a projectile experiences a constant horizontal velocity and a uniform vertical acceleration due to gravity (g = 9.81 m/s², downward).

Choosing a Cartesian coordinate frame with positive x directed horizontally forward and positive y directed vertically upward (aₓ = 0 m/s², aᵧ = -g = -9.81 m/s²), the initial launch velocity vector v₀ angled at θ above the horizontal resolves into perpendicular components:

v₀ₓ = v₀ · cos(θ)
v₀ᵧ = v₀ · sin(θ)

Because horizontal acceleration is zero, horizontal displacement (Δx) depends linearly on total flight time (Δt):

Δx = v₀ₓ · Δt = (v₀ · cos(θ)) · Δt

Vertical displacement (Δy) is governed by constant-acceleration kinematics:

Δy = v₀ᵧ · Δt - ½g(Δt)² = (v₀ · sin(θ)) · Δt - ½g(Δt)²

Equal Launch and Landing Heights (Δy = 0)

When a projectile lands at the same height from which it was released (Δy = 0), solving the vertical displacement equation for non-zero time yields total flight time:

Δt = (2v₀ · sin(θ)) / g

Substituting Δt into the horizontal displacement equation gives the classical range equation:

R = (v₀² · sin(2θ)) / g

For a fixed launch speed v₀, range is maximized when sin(2θ) = 1, corresponding to an optimal launch angle of θ = 45°. Furthermore, complementary angles (θ and 90° - θ) yield identical theoretical ranges.

Unequal Launch and Landing Heights (Δy ≠ 0)

When landing height differs from launch height, total flight time must be determined by solving the quadratic vertical motion equation:

-½g(Δt)² + (v₀ · sin(θ))Δt - Δy = 0

Applying the quadratic formula yields the physically meaningful positive root for flight time:

Δt = [v₀ · sin(θ) + √(v₀² · sin²(θ) - 2gΔy)] / g

The resulting horizontal range is:

R = v₀ · cos(θ) · [ [v₀ · sin(θ) + √(v₀² · sin²(θ) - 2gΔy)] / g ]

  • Desk to Ground (Δy < 0): Negative displacement increases flight time, causing horizontal range to increase at every angle and shifting optimal launch angle below 45°.

  • Ground to Desk (Δy > 0): Positive displacement reduces flight time, causing horizontal range to decrease at every angle and shifting optimal launch angle above 45°.

Purpose

To investigate the effect of launch angle (θ = 25°, 40°, 55°) and vertical displacement (Δy = 0 m, -0.75 m, +0.40 m) on the horizontal range (R) of a projectile, and to compare experimental observations against theoretical predictions derived from 2-D kinematic equations.

Hypothesis

  1. Desk-to-Desk (Δy = 0 m): Horizontal range is predicted to follow R = (v02 · sin(2θ)) / g, maximizing at 45°. Among the tested angles (25°, 40°, 55°), 40° will yield the longest range because it is closest to 45°. 25° will yield the shortest range (sin(50°) = 0.766), while 55° (sin(110°) = 0.940) will fall between 25° and 40°.

  2. Desk-to-Ground (Δy = -0.75 m): Descending an additional height h = 0.75 m will extend flight time across all angles, producing greater horizontal ranges than the corresponding Desk-to-Desk trials. The optimal launch angle will shift below 45°; 40° is predicted to yield the longest range, with 25° demonstrating the largest relative percentage increase due to low initial vertical velocity.

  3. Ground-to-Desk (Δy = +0.40 m): Climbing an upward height Δh = +0.40 m will curtail flight time, producing shorter horizontal ranges across all angles compared to Desk-to-Desk trials. The optimal launch angle will shift above 45°. The low 25° launch will suffer the largest reduction because its maximum vertical clearance barely exceeds landing height.

Variables

  • Independent Variables:

    • Launch angle (θ), varied at 25°, 40°, 55° (±1°).

    • Height configuration setup, altering vertical displacement (Δy = 0 m, -0.75 m, +0.40 m).

  • Dependent Variable:

    • Horizontal range (R), measured in meters (±0.005 m tape uncertainty; trial spread uncertainty ±0.035 m to ±0.065 m).

  • Controlled Variables:

    • Launcher compression setting (kept on fixed spring detent/Long Range mode).

    • Projectile mass and diameter (16 mm steel sphere).

    • Alignment and levelness of launch platform and landing surfaces.

    • Gravitational acceleration (g = 9.81 m/s²).

Materials

  • Spring-loaded mini projectile launcher (MPL001) with integrated angle protractor and plumb bob.

  • 16 mm steel sphere projectile.

  • Two desks (height h = 0.75 m ± 0.005 m).

  • Measuring tape (30 m roll, ±0.005 m precision) and meter sticks.

  • Wood block for vertical axis calibration.

Safety Precautions

  • Wear protective safety goggles at all times during launcher setup and trial execution.

  • Ensure the trajectory path and landing zones remain clear of personnel prior to triggering the launch mechanism.

  • Do not look directly down the barrel of the launcher when loaded or cocked.

Procedure

  1. Desk-to-Desk Setup (Δy = 0 m):

    • Secure the projectile launcher to the edge of a level desk using a C-clamp. Mount a receiving desk at equal height directly along the firing axis.

    • Verify using a plumb line that the zero mark aligns vertically beneath the muzzle's release point.

    • Adjust the launcher to θ = 25° using the integrated protractor scale. Load the 16 mm steel ball to the predetermined spring compression setting.

    • Fire the projectile, measure the landing mark distance from the muzzle origin, and record the trial.

    • Repeat for 3 trials at 25°, 40°, and 55°.

  1. Desk-to-Ground Setup (Δy = -0.75 m):

    • Keep the launcher clamped to the desk edge (h = 0.75 m ± 0.005 m).

    • Perform 3 launch trials each at 25°, 40°, and 55°. Measure horizontal distance from the plumb line origin to the carbon mark on the floor.

  1. Ground-to-Desk Setup (Δy = +0.40 m):

    • Position the launcher on a stable ground plate below a receiving desk elevated Δh = 0.40 m ± 0.01 m above the muzzle launch line.

    • Perform 3 launch trials each at 25°, 40°, and 55°, measuring horizontal range from origin to impact point on the desk.

Qualitative Observations

  • Auditory feedback from the launcher spring mechanism remained consistent across all trials.

  • Impact marks on carbon paper formed distinct single-point impressions, grouped tightly within a 7 cm to 13 cm window per angle series.

  • Measurement readings were taken at the initial impact point, eliminating bounce artifacts.

Analysis and Sample Calculations

A. Launch Velocity Determination (v₀)

Using equal-height Desk-to-Desk mean experimental ranges (R) and rearranging R = (v₀² · sin(2θ)) / g:

v₀ = √[ (R · g) / sin(2θ) ]

  1. For θ = 25° (R = 3.760 m):
    v₀, ₂₅° = √[ (3.760 m · 9.81 m/s²) / sin(50°) ] = √(36.8856 / 0.76604) = 6.939 m/s

  2. For θ = 40° (R = 4.570 m):
    v₀, ₄₀° = √[ (4.570 m · 9.81 m/s²) / sin(80°) ] = √(44.8317 / 0.98481) = 6.747 m/s

  3. For θ = 55° (R = 4.350 m):
    v₀, ₅₅° = √[ (4.350 m · 9.81 m/s²) / sin(110°) ] = √(42.6735 / 0.93969) = 6.739 m/s

Mean Baseline Launch Speed:
v₀ = (6.939 + 6.747 + 6.739) / 3 = 6.808 m/s ≈ 6.81 m/s
(v₀² = 46.376 m²/s²)

Theoretical Sample Calculations

Sample 1: Desk to Desk (θ = 40°, Δy = 0 m)
Rₜₕₑₒ = (v₀² · sin(2θ)) / g = (46.376 · sin(80°)) / 9.81 = (46.376 · 0.98481) / 9.81 = 4.655 m
Percent Error = [ (Rₑₓₚ - Rₜₕₑₒ) / Rₜₕₑₒ ] · 100% = [ (4.570 - 4.655) / 4.655 ] · 100% = -1.83% ≈ -1.9%

Sample 2: Desk to Ground (θ = 40°, Δy = -0.75 m)

  1. Velocity Components:
    v₀ₓ = 6.808 · cos(40°) = 5.215 m/s
    v₀ᵧ = 6.808 · sin(40°) = 4.376 m/s

  2. Flight Time (Δt):
    Δt = [ 4.376 + √(4.376² - 2(9.81)(-0.75)) ] / 9.81 = [ 4.376 + √(19.150 + 14.715) ] / 9.81 = 1.039 s

  3. Theoretical Range (Rₜₕₑₒ):
    Rₜₕₑₒ = v₀ₓ · Δt = 5.215 m/s · 1.039 s = 5.418 m

  4. Percent Error:
    Percent Error = [ (5.340 - 5.418) / 5.418 ] · 100% = -1.44% ≈ -1.4%

Sample 3: Ground to Desk (θ = 40°, Δy = +0.40 m)

  1. Flight Time (Δt):
    Δt = [ 4.376 + √(4.376² - 2(9.81)(0.40)) ] / 9.81 = [ 4.376 + √(19.150 - 7.848) ] / 9.81 = 0.789 s

  2. Theoretical Range (Rₜₕₑₒ):
    Rₜₕₑₒ = v₀ₓ · Δt = 5.215 m/s · 0.789 s = 4.115 m

  3. Percent Error:
    Percent Error = [ (3.800 - 4.115) / 4.115 ] · 100% = -7.65% ≈ -7.7%

Discussion

Influence of Launch Angle on Range

For Desk-to-Desk launches (Δy = 0), horizontal range depends directly on the product of horizontal velocity component (v₀ · cos(θ)) and flight duration (Δt = (2v₀ · sin(θ)) / g). Increasing launch angle increases vertical flight time but decreases forward horizontal velocity. The maximum product occurs at 45°. Among experimental trials, 40° produced the maximum range (4.570 m), outperforming 55° (4.350 m) and 25° (3.760 m). This confirms theoretical expectations: 40° deviates by only 5° from the 45° optimum (sin(80°) = 0.985), whereas 55° deviates by 10° (sin(110°) = 0.940).

Influence of Elevation Difference

  1. Desk to Ground (Δy = -0.75 m): Releasing the projectile above the landing surface extends vertical fall time. At θ = 25°, fall time increased total flight duration from 0.587 s to 0.782 s (+33.2%), increasing horizontal range from 3.760 m to 5.200 m (+38.3%). Because extra fall height adds time independently of initial vertical speed, the optimal launch angle shifts below 45°, confirming Hypothesis 2.

  2. Ground to Desk (Δy = +0.40 m): Releasing below the landing surface requires the projectile to climb against gravity, shortening flight time. At θ = 25°, total flight duration dropped to 0.361 s (range 2.400 m), because the peak apex height (yₘₐₓ = v₀ᵧ² / 2g = (2.878)² / 19.62 = 0.422 m) barely cleared the 0.40 m landing height. This confirms Hypothesis 3.

Evaluation of Hypotheses

All three hypotheses were fully supported by experimental evidence:

  • Hypothesis 1 (Desk to Desk): Confirmed (40° > 55° > 25°).

  • Hypothesis 2 (Desk to Ground): Confirmed (all ranges increased; maximum range at 40° = 5.340 m).

  • Hypothesis 3 (Ground to Desk): Confirmed (all ranges decreased; 25° exhibited the largest reduction).

Error Analysis and Experimental Improvements

Systematic Error Analysis

  1. Aerodynamic Drag: Air resistance introduces a retarding force proportional to v². This systematically reduces horizontal velocity over time, causing experimental ranges at higher speeds and angles (40°, 55°) to fall consistently below ideal vacuum predictions (e.g., -11.2% error at 55° Ground to Desk).

  2. Muzzle Release Height Offset: Clamping the launcher to a tabletop places the release point slightly above the table surface (+2 cm to +3 cm). In Desk-to-Desk trials, this extra height slightly extended flight time, causing low-angle launches (25°) to overshoot ideal equal-height predictions (+3.8% error).

  3. Protractor Alignment: Reading the launcher protractor carries a systematic/random limit of ±1°. At shallow angles (θ = 25°), a 1° variance alters sin(2θ) by ~3.2%, contributing to higher percent errors at 25°.

Random Error Analysis

  • Spring Release Variations: Minor friction fluctuations in the trigger detent induce slight shot-to-shot velocity variations (±0.10 m/s).

Table 5: Error Analysis and Proposed Methodological Improvements

Identified Source of Error Error Type Impact on Results Proposed Experimental Improvement
Aerodynamic drag Systematic Reduces horizontal speed; causes Rₑₓₚ < Rₜₕₑₒ at high angles Use denser, smaller steel projectiles or photogate trajectory modeling
Muzzle elevation offset Systematic Adds unexpected Δy in equal-height setups; inflates low-angle range Measure effective release origin using a plumb line directly from muzzle center
Protractor precision (±1°) Systematic / Random Alters velocity components; highest sensitivity at 25° Attach a digital angle finder (±0.1° resolution) to launcher barrel

Conclusion

The experimental objectives were successfully fulfilled. Horizontal range in two-dimensional projectile motion was demonstrated to depend fundamentally on launch angle (θ) and vertical displacement (Δy). For equal-height launches, range was maximized at 40° (4.570 m), agreeing with theoretical kinematic predictions (4.655 m, -1.8% error) and an estimated baseline launch speed v0 = 6.81 m/s. Descending vertical displacement (Δy = -0.75 m) increased flight time and horizontal range across all angles (peaking at 5.340 m for 40°), whereas ascending vertical displacement (Δy = +0.40 m) shortened flight time (reducing 25° range to 2.400 m). Experimental observations aligned with theoretical models within 1.4% to 11.2%, with deviations explained by air resistance, muzzle height offset, and measurement uncertainty.
